cells.tense: You are in this now, seeing it whole, and you know writing it down is what keeps it steady.
cells.ask: Write one sentence about what you see now, not what you saw before. Put it down. Glance at it tomorrow and add a second.
cells.core:
You can see this whole, and you can hold it while it's still unfinished. Nothing here is hidden from you, and you haven't needed a verdict to keep the picture steady. That's the part in good order.

What you see doesn't finish the thing by itself. The ending still gets walked, and on the way people will hand you their versions of what happened. Keep the sentences that still ring true in a week and set the others down. Write more than you show anyone — a page holds what you see until you're ready to say it out loud.
cells.sheetLine: You can see it whole. Writing it down is how it holds.
cells.place: in the room where something has to end

cells.tense: You are fixed on a resolution you refuse to let arrive on its own timing, rehearsing it before the ground is laid.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're trying to settle right now and leave it alone for a day. No plans, no verdict. Let it sit unfocused.
cells.core:
You're trying to close this ahead of when it can close. The bracing is spending you — rehearsing the last word before it has to be said, treating what's still forming as if it were already decided.

The clean version of this is quieter. You stand in the open part with what you know and let it stay open, because nothing has to be pushed to stay true, and whatever hasn't arrived yet catches fire on its own when it's ready. Keep today unscheduled. Nothing you've seen goes away because you waited a day to use it.
cells.sheetLine: You're closing this before it's ready to close.

cells.tense: You are standing at a door that has already closed behind you, still deciding whether to turn the handle.
cells.ask: Name one thing that looks finished to you. Write it on a scrap, put the scrap in a drawer, and act on nothing this week.
cells.core:
Nothing has shifted on this question in a while, or you wouldn't keep reopening it. When nothing gets set down, everything stays live, and finished and unfinished come to feel the same in the hand. You can see what each piece is; the move to match hasn't come.

Pick one piece and say what it looks like to you. Not the plan, not the speech — just the thing itself, named and set on paper, so you can look at it there. Naming one thing changes what sits at the front, and the rest of the pile starts to hold a little.
cells.sheetLine: The picture is here. The move isn't yet.

cells.tense: You have already put something down, and you keep speaking as if it were still strapped to your back.
cells.ask: Next time you describe what you've been through, add where it stands now. Say the current part out loud, once.
cells.core:
You tell this in the past tense and describe it as a weight you're still under. But notice how you sleep, or how this lands when the subject comes around — the pull isn't there anymore. The ending ran somewhere you weren't watching. That's fine; endings do that.

It isn't that your account is wrong, only that it hasn't caught up. When it does, what happened and what's true today sit in the same sentence, and you can say both without bracing. One line gets both ends on it: what it was, and where it stands now. Nothing needs to be built on that yet.
cells.sheetLine: You already put it down. You're still calling it heavy.
